title: Static Routing: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: Who tells a router where to send traffic? Sometimes, you do. By simply writing it down.

lines.t: Who tells the router where to go?

scenes.heading: The note in the mailroom
scenes.narration: Picture an office mailroom. The building manager writes a note. All packages for Accounting go to floor three. That note is a static route. It stays put until the manager changes it. If Accounting moves, the note is wrong, and packages go missing. The mailroom clerk never learns, they just follow the note.

scenes.heading: Writing a static route
scenes.narration: The command is I P route, then the network, then the mask, then where to send it. A route to zero zero zero zero is the default route. And add a bigger number on the end, and you get a backup, called a floating static route.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three common slip-ups. Static routes do not update themselves when a link fails. The default distance is one, but you can change it. And the mask must be written in dotted form, not as a slash.

items.wrong: Static routes update when a link fails
items.right: They never adapt on their own
Default is 1, but you can set it

items.wrong: You can write /24 in ip route

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.cta: Try the Courseiva static routing lab
scenes.narration: So, to recap. A static route is a note you write by hand. A default route sends everything unknown one way. And a higher distance turns it into a backup. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva static routing lab.

points.t: A static route is a hand-written note
